easy.heading: Starting Small and Sweet
easy.body:
I started today's session with the easy puzzle and it was a great way to wake up the brain. The first things I noticed were the sum targets of 0 at cells [2,0] and [3,4]. Since you cannot have negative pips, those spots had to be 0! This made it easy to place the [0,3] and [0,6] dominoes. I put the [0,3] domino across [2,0] and [2,1], and the [0,6] domino across [3,3] and [3,4].

Next, I looked at the equals constraint between [2,3] and [3,3]. Since I just placed a 6 at [3,3], I knew [2,3] also had to be a 6. That meant the [6,5] domino had to go in cells [2,3] and [2,4]. After that, the rest fell into place. I used the [2,2] domino for the less than 6 area at the top and the [4,3] domino to satisfy the less than 4 constraint at the bottom. It felt like a quick win!

medium.heading: Mid-Morning Brain Teaser
medium.body:
The medium puzzle definitely stepped things up. That big sum of 20 across cells [0,1], [0,2], [1,2], and [1,3] was a total beacon. To get a sum that high with only four cells, you really need to use your heaviest hitters. I realized the [6,4] and [5,5] dominoes were going to be the stars of the show in that upper-middle section.

I had a little trouble around the sum 4 constraint at [0,0] and [1,0] until I looked at the bottom. The sum of 10 for [2,1] and [2,2] was another clear sign to use the [5,5] domino there. Once I cleared the bottom row, it was much easier to see that the [1,2] domino had to sit vertically to satisfy the sum constraints on the left side. It took a bit of back-and-forth, but seeing those big numbers click into place is so satisfying.

hard.heading: A Triple Shot Espresso Challenge
hard.body:
Wow, the hard puzzle was a real workout! The standout feature was that long chain of equals constraints. Cells [1,0], [2,0], [3,0], and [4,0] all had to have the same number of pips. This meant I had to find four different dominoes that all shared a common value. I eventually figured out that 5 was the magic number for that column, which let me place dominoes like [5,0] and [5,2] effectively.

Another tricky spot was the bottom right where [6,3], [6,4], and [6,5] were all equal. I used the [6,6] domino and part of the [6,4] domino to make that work. The hardest part for me was the top row sum of 8 for [0,4] and [0,5]. I kept trying different combinations until I realized the [5,3] domino was the only one left that fit the pips I had available. It was a slow process of elimination, but the logic was rock solid in the end.

explanation.tips: Always look for the zeros first because they act like anchors for your dominoes. If you see a high sum target, grab your dominoes with the most pips and see if they fit there first. Don't be afraid to work from the corners inward, as those constraints often have fewer possibilities than the ones in the middle of the grid.
explanation.learned: Today I learned how powerful equal constraints can be when they are chained together in a row or column. It forces you to look at your entire inventory of dominoes to find a common number, rather than just looking at one piece at a time. I also noticed that high sums are great for narrowing down the [6,6] and [5,5] pieces early on, which clears up a lot of clutter on your board.

faqs.question: How do you solve NYT Pips puzzle?
faqs.answer: You solve it by placing dominoes onto a grid so that the numbers of pips match the mathematical constraints like sums, equals, or less-than symbols shown in specific regions.

faqs.question: What does a sum target of 0 mean in Pips?
faqs.answer: A sum target of 0 means the cell must contain a domino side with zero pips, which is the blank side of a domino.

faqs.question: Can dominoes be placed vertically or horizontally in Pips?
faqs.answer: Yes, dominoes can be placed in either orientation as long as they cover two adjacent cells and satisfy the regional rules.

faqs.question: What is the best strategy for the hard Pips puzzle?
faqs.answer: Focus on the equals constraints that span multiple cells first. These often limit your choices significantly and reveal which number must repeat across those dominoes.

faqs.question: Are all dominoes in the list used in every Pips puzzle?
faqs.answer: Yes, every domino provided in the daily list must be placed exactly once on the board to complete the puzzle.
